author: Declaration Desk
title: Bangladesh garment wage board agrees new minimum pay will take effect from December
dek: Owners and workers agreed the timetable at the board's first meeting, but not the amount; workers want Tk 30,000 a month, and clashes went on in Savar and Gazipur on the fifth day of protests.

body:
Bangladesh's new minimum wage board for garment workers agreed at its first meeting in Dhaka on Wednesday that a revised minimum wage will take effect in December, with workers receiving the higher pay in their January salaries. The board has not yet decided how much the new wage will be. Workers want the monthly minimum raised to Tk 30,000 from Tk 12,500.

The timetable was announced after the meeting by the board's new chairman, Syed Azad Subhani, and confirmed by the representatives of both sides, The Business Standard (TBS) and Daily Waadaa reported. Outside the capital, protests went on for a fifth day: Reuters reported clashes between workers and police in Savar and Gazipur, two garment hubs on Dhaka's outskirts, where demonstrators blocked roads and police used tear gas and sound grenades.

## What the board agreed

The meeting began at about 11.30 am Dhaka time (11 am IST) at the board's office in Segunbagicha, according to Daily Waadaa. Subhani, who was appointed after the first chairman, Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman, stepped down, described the talks as productive.

"New wages will be implemented in December. Workers will receive their new salaries from January," Babul Akter, a workers' representative on the board and general secretary of the Bangladesh Garment and Industrial Workers Federation, told TBS. He said employers had accepted the workers' demand on timing. ABM Shamsuddin, an owners' representative, agreed with that account, TBS reported. Babul Akter then urged workers to return to their factories.

He told Daily Waadaa that the board would "have to sit again with the stakeholders" to discuss the workers' proposals before deciding on an amount. The board must weigh competing proposals from workers and employers and recommend new rates; these then go through the statutory approval and gazette process before they become legally binding. The meeting was convened under Section 139 of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006. No date for the next meeting was announced.

Workers also want an end to the blacklisting of workers and to what they call unjust layoffs, TBS reported.

## Protests and factory closures

The unrest began last week in Mirpur and spread to Gazipur, Ashulia, Savar and Narayanganj. Several factories suspended operations again on Wednesday because of fears of further trouble, Reuters reported; no overall count for the day had been published by the time of writing. The manufacturers' association BGMEA said 306 factories had suspended production on Tuesday, affecting nearly 7 lakh workers: 161 in Gazipur and Mymensingh, 93 in Savar, Ashulia and Zirabo, and 52 in Mirpur, according to Daily Waadaa. BGMEA had put the number disrupted on Sunday at 529. Counts differ by source and are approximate.

Over the weekend and on Monday, workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway and the Dhaka-Narayanganj link road, a police vehicle was set on fire under a Mirpur metro station, and police used batons, tear gas, sound grenades and water cannon, according to The Daily Star, Prothom Alo, AFP and Reuters. At least 20 people, including four or five police officers, were injured in Mirpur on Sunday, Bangladesh Post reported. The government deployed Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) in Gazipur's industrial areas, where it says it will stay until 7 November.

Factory owners had threatened to keep units in unrest-hit areas closed, but agreed to reopen them on Wednesday at the government's request, TBS reported. A BGMEA vice-president, Mijanur Rahman, said owners could still shut factories that faced continued violence under Section 13(1) of the Labour Act, which allows a suspension without pay.

## Claims about the Awami League

Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has blamed factory owners linked to the former Awami League government for fuelling the unrest, The Daily Star reported, and a Dhaka Metropolitan Police official told TBS that 33 members of the banned party and its affiliates had been arrested in 24 hours on suspicion of posing as workers to cause sabotage. Neither the minister nor the police made evidence public, and the Awami League had not responded. Labour leaders say the protests have been largely spontaneous, and bdnews24 reported that workers have often taken to the streets without unions.

## Background

Garments earn more than 80% of Bangladesh's export income, about $38.7 billion in the year to June 2026, and employ about four million people, TBS reported. Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter after China, supplying brands such as H&M, Zara and Walmart. The current minimum of Tk 12,500 was set in December 2023, up from Tk 8,000, after protests that year. The Tk 30,000 now demanded would be a rise of 140%.

Owners cite higher costs, uncertainty in energy markets linked to the war in the Middle East and softer demand in export markets. Workers point to rising prices and a recent pay rise for government employees. "Every month is a struggle," one worker, Bithi Begum, told Reuters. H&M told Reuters that some factories had closed temporarily but that it had not seen major supply-chain disruption.

Selim Raihan, an economist at Dhaka University, told Reuters that Bangladesh could absorb a significant wage increase without losing its edge if productivity improved, and that prolonged unrest was a greater threat than higher wages. "Treating cheap labour as the industry's permanent competitive strategy would be a mistake," he said.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

India's apparel exporters compete with Bangladesh for orders from the same global brands, and buyers worried about delays may look elsewhere in the region. Bangladesh also buys cotton, yarn and fabric from India, much of it by road through West Bengal's Petrapole-Benapole crossing, so a long shutdown would hit traders and transporters on the Indian side. India's external affairs ministry said on Tuesday that it was monitoring the protests.

Officials of the two countries are due to meet in Dhaka on 17 and 18 November, when Bangladesh says it will raise the extradition of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

## What happens next

- The wage board meets again to weigh proposals from workers and owners; no date has been set.
- The new minimum wage is to take effect in December and show in January pay, once it is gazetted.
- BGB personnel stay in Gazipur's industrial areas until 7 November.
- Indian and Bangladeshi officials meet in Dhaka on 17 and 18 November.

## Key numbers

- Tk 30,000: the monthly minimum wage workers want
- Tk 12,500: the current minimum, set in December 2023
- 306: factories that suspended production on Tuesday (BGMEA, via Daily Waadaa)
- 529: factories disrupted on Sunday (BGMEA)
- 4 million: garment workers in Bangladesh
- 80%+: garments' share of Bangladesh's export earnings
